taxonomyNote: NatureServe: split by McDonough et al. (2022) into western spotted skunk (S. gracilis) and desert spotted skunk (S. leucoparia).
fieldMarks: Small and slender, black with white spots on the forehead and in front of each ear
Stripes: dorsolateral pair from the back of the head, a lateral pair joining the ear spots, and a ventrolateral pair; they end at mid-body
Rear body has two interrupted white bands, a white rump spot each side and two at the tail base
Underside of tail white for nearly half its length, tip extensively white
Males about 423 mm and 565 g; females about 360 mm and 368 g
behavior: More nocturnal than the striped skunk and rarely seen by day; active year round
Eats insects, rodents, small birds, possibly eggs, reptiles, amphibians, fruit and berries
Dens in rocks, burrows, hollow logs, brush piles and under buildings
habitat: Brushy canyons, rocky outcrops and canyon walls; rocky bluffs and brush-bordered canyon stream beds; sometimes nests in rock fences or attics.
range: Much of the western United States, including the Channel Islands of California, and the Baja Peninsula.

lookalikes.name: Eastern spotted skunk
lookalikes.howToTell: Looks similar but with less extensive white.
